interest: Colombia shares intelligence with the U.S. on Japanese oil and mining interests.
overview: This file (State Department decimal 894.20221) documents United States diplomatic and military intelligence surveillance of Japanese commercial, agricultural, and covert activities in Colombia between 1932 and 1940, driven predominantly by strategic concerns over the defense of the Panama Canal and adjacent waterways. Early inquiries in 1932 investigated rumors that Japanese operatives disguised as fishermen were conducting clandestine coastal and hydrographic surveys along Colombia's Caribbean and Pacific coasts, though American consular officers found no supporting evidence at the time. By 1936–1938, as geopolitical tensions escalated in Asia and Europe, surveillance intensified around Japanese attempts to purchase Colombian oil reserves and government royalty crude, acquire platinum and gold mining concessions in the Chocó and Nariño departments, and establish agricultural colonies such as the Corinto settlement in the Cauca Valley. The file highlights close surveillance of Japanese engineers and corporate emissaries affiliated with the Mitsui Company and Kaigai Kōgyō Kaisha, their interactions with German nationals and the German-Colombian airline SCADTA, and high-level bilateral diplomacy in which Colombian Presidents Alfonso López Pumarejo and Eduardo Santos sought joint coastal surveillance and requested United States naval and aviation military missions to help safeguard national territory.

subfiles.about: State Department instruction directing the Legation in Bogotá to discreetly investigate reports of Japanese topographical and hydrographic surveys along Latin American coasts.

subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 345 tells Bogotá to check reports of Japanese fishermen surveying Latin American coasts.

subfiles.to: Allan Dawson, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Bogotá

subfiles.about: Legation despatch reporting that comprehensive inquiries by U.S. consular officers along Colombia's Pacific and Caribbean coasts found no evidence of Japanese surveys or fishermen.

subfiles.summary: Dawson reports that consuls found no Japanese fishermen on Colombia's coasts.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3772 from Bogotá on Alleged Japanese Activities on Colombian Coasts
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Military intelligence report regarding the suspicious presence and surveillance activities of three Japanese visitors during a U.S. naval courtesy visit to Buenaventura.

subfiles.summary: Military Attaché reports three Japanese, including Yuzo Takeshima, watching reactions to a U.S. naval visit at Buenaventura in 1936.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report on Japanese Activities in Buenaventura During U.S. Naval Visit

subfiles.about: Naval intelligence report detailing the acreage and estimated population of the Japanese agricultural colony established at Corinto, Valle del Cauca.

subfiles.title: Naval Attaché Report No. 254-1937 on Japanese Agricultural Colony at Corinto
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department

subfiles.about: Naval intelligence report detailing Japanese diplomatic and commercial maneuvers to purchase crude petroleum and Colombian government royalty oil.

subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department
